title: Typing Versus Writing: Laptop Note-Taking and Conceptual Understanding of Lectures
based_on: Mueller, P. A., & Oppenheimer, D. M. (2014). The pen is mightier than the keyboard: Advantages of longhand over laptop note taking. Psychological Science, 25(6), 1159–1168. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797614524581

s: Laptops are now common in university lecture halls, and many students prefer typing their notes because it is faster than writing by hand.
This study tested whether taking notes on a laptop or by hand affects how well students learn from a lecture.
Students watched short talks and took notes either on a laptop or with pen and paper, and then answered factual and conceptual questions about the talks.
Both groups performed similarly on factual questions, but students who wrote by hand performed better on conceptual questions.
Laptop notes contained more words copied word-for-word from the talks, which was linked to poorer conceptual performance.
These results suggest that typing notes may lead to shallower processing of lecture material.
Taking notes is one of the most common ways that students try to learn during lectures.
Note-taking is thought to help learning in two ways: by helping students process information as they write it down, and by giving them a record to review later.
Today, many students take notes on laptops instead of on paper.
Laptops allow students to type quickly and to record more of what the lecturer says.
However, laptops can also distract students, for example through social media and online shopping.
Studies have found that students who use laptops in class often spend part of the lecture on activities unrelated to the course, and that this multitasking is linked to lower grades.
Even students sitting near a laptop user may be distracted by what is on their classmate's screen.
Most research on laptops in class has focused on these distractions, and much less is known about whether typing notes changes learning even when students are not distracted.
In this study, conceptual understanding refers to the ability to explain ideas, apply them and see how they relate to one another, rather than simply remembering facts.
Verbatim note-taking refers to copying down the speaker's words exactly as they are said, rather than summarising them in one's own words.

One explanation for why the type of note-taking might matter comes from the levels-of-processing framework (Craik & Lockhart, 1972), which proposes that information that is processed more deeply, in terms of its meaning, is remembered better.

Because students cannot write as fast as a lecturer speaks, those writing by hand must select and summarise, which may encourage deeper processing, whereas fast typists may simply copy the lecturer's words.
The present study asked whether taking notes on a laptop, compared with taking notes by hand, affects students' factual and conceptual learning from a lecture.
It was hypothesised that students who took notes by hand would perform better on conceptual questions than students who took notes on laptops.
The study was an experiment in which students were randomly assigned to take notes either on a laptop or with pen and paper.
Participants were 67 undergraduate students at Princeton University who took part for course credit.
Laptops were provided by the researchers and were disconnected from the internet, so that distraction could not explain any differences.
Participants watched one of five TED talks of about 15 minutes each on interesting but not commonly known topics, while taking notes in the way they normally would using their assigned method.
After the talk, participants completed distracting tasks for 30 minutes before answering questions about the talk.
Factual questions asked participants to recall specific details from the talk, such as dates or names, whereas conceptual questions asked them to explain or apply ideas from the talk.
Verbatim note-taking was measured by using computer software to count how many three-word sequences in each participant's notes exactly matched the words in the talk.
Students in the two conditions performed equally well on factual questions, with no significant difference between them.
Students who took notes by hand performed significantly better on conceptual questions than students who used laptops, p < .05.
Laptop users wrote more words in total than students writing by hand.
However, laptop notes also contained a significantly higher proportion of words copied verbatim from the talk.
The more verbatim overlap participants' notes contained, the worse they performed on conceptual questions.
These results show that taking notes on a laptop may harm conceptual learning, even when students are not distracted by the internet.
Laptop users seemed to transcribe the lectures rather than process and reframe the information in their own words.
Writing more notes would normally be expected to help learning, because students have more information to review later.
In this study, however, the advantage of having more notes seems to have been outweighed by the shallower processing involved in copying the lecturer's words.
These findings support the levels-of-processing framework, as summarising in one's own words appears to involve deeper processing than copying.
In practice, students who use laptops in lectures could be encouraged to summarise ideas in their own words rather than typing everything the lecturer says.
One limitation is that participants answered questions shortly after the talk without the chance to review their notes, which is not how students usually prepare for exams.
Future studies could examine whether the benefits of handwritten notes remain when students are given time to study their notes before being tested.
Overall, the results suggest that the pen may be mightier than the keyboard when it comes to understanding.

title: Remembering Where You Learned: Context-Dependent Memory in Divers on Land and Underwater
short: Divers' memory on land vs underwater
based_on: Godden, D. R., & Baddeley, A. D. (1975). Context-dependent memory in two natural environments: On land and underwater. British Journal of Psychology, 66(3), 325–331. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2044-8295.1975.tb01468.x

s: Many people find it easier to remember something when they return to the place where they first learned it.
This study tested whether memory is better when information is recalled in the same environment in which it was learned.
Divers learned lists of words either on a beach or underwater and then recalled them either in the same environment or in the other one.
Words were recalled better when the learning and recall environments matched than when they did not.
These results provide strong evidence for context-dependent memory in natural environments.
Everyday experience suggests that the place where we learn something can help us remember it.
For example, people sometimes forget why they walked into a room, but remember again when they go back to where they started.
Context-dependent memory refers to the finding that information is easier to recall when the physical environment at recall matches the environment in which it was learned.

This idea is explained by the encoding specificity principle (Tulving & Thomson, 1973), which states that memory is best when the cues present at retrieval match the cues present when the information was first encoded.
According to this principle, features of the environment, such as sights and sounds, become stored together with what is learned and can later act as retrieval cues.
Earlier laboratory studies found some evidence for context effects, for instance when the colour or smell of a room was changed between learning and testing.
Other studies have found that people's internal state, such as their mood, can also act as a context, so that information learned while happy is easier to recall when happy again.
These findings suggest that memories are stored together with information about the situation in which they were formed.
However, most of these studies used small changes in context within a laboratory, and their results were often weak or inconsistent.
Very few studies had tested context-dependent memory in two very different natural environments.
Divers offer a useful opportunity to do this, because being underwater is extremely different from being on land, in terms of sight, sound, temperature and breathing.
The present study asked whether divers would recall words better when they were tested in the same environment in which they had learned them.
It was hypothesised that recall would be higher when the learning and recall environments were the same than when they were different.
The study was an experiment in which every participant took part in all four combinations of learning environment and recall environment.
Participants were 18 members of a university diving club, who took part during a diving trip in Scotland.

Each participant learned four lists of 36 unrelated words, each list in one of four conditions: learn on land and recall on land, learn on land and recall underwater, learn underwater and recall underwater, and learn underwater and recall on land.
Words were presented through a tape recorder, and when on land, divers sat at the edge of the water wearing their diving equipment, so that the only difference between conditions was the environment.
The order of the conditions was varied across participants, so that tiredness or practice could not explain the results.
Recall was measured by asking participants to write down as many words as they could remember from each list, and the score was the number of words correctly recalled.
When words were learned and recalled in the same environment, participants recalled an average of about 13 words.
When words were learned in one environment and recalled in the other, participants recalled an average of about 8.5 words.
This difference was statistically significant, p < .05, and represents roughly 40% better recall when the environments matched.
The effect was found both for words learned on land and for words learned underwater.
The results show that recall was clearly better when divers were tested in the same environment where they had learned the words.
The size of this effect is notable, as a 40% difference is much larger than the effects found in earlier laboratory studies of context.
This may be because being underwater is so different from being on land that it provides many distinctive cues that can later help or hinder recall.
These findings support the encoding specificity principle, suggesting that environmental cues are stored with memories and help people retrieve them.
In practice, divers who are trained on land may need to practise important procedures underwater, and students may benefit from studying in conditions similar to those of the exam.
One limitation is that the sample was small, with only 18 divers, all of whom were experienced members of one diving club.
Future research could examine whether simply imagining the learning environment can produce the same memory benefits as being physically present.
These results show that where we learn something can have a large influence on what we later remember.

title: Out of Sight, Out of Mind? Smartphone Location and Available Cognitive Capacity
based_on: Ward, A. F., Duke, K., Gneezy, A., & Bos, M. W. (2017). Brain drain: The mere presence of one's own smartphone reduces available cognitive capacity. Journal of the Association for Consumer Research, 2(2), 140–154. https://doi.org/10.1086/691462

s: Smartphones give people constant access to information and entertainment, and many people keep their phones close at all times.
This study tested whether simply having one's own smartphone nearby, even when it is switched off, reduces the mental capacity available for other tasks.
Participants completed tests of working memory and reasoning while their phones were on the desk, in their pocket or bag, or in another room.
Participants whose phones were in another room performed best on the working memory test, and those whose phones were on the desk performed worst.
These results suggest that the mere presence of a smartphone can drain cognitive capacity.
Most adults now own a smartphone, and many check their phones dozens of times each day.
Smartphones are useful, but they may also compete for attention, for example through notifications and the temptation to check messages.
Previous research has shown that phone notifications and phone use can interrupt work and reduce performance.
For example, students who receive text messages during a lecture tend to remember less of the lecture than students who do not.
Even hearing a phone ring or vibrate can make it harder to concentrate, because it reminds people of messages they may be missing.
However, little research has examined whether a smartphone can affect thinking when it is silent, switched off and not being used at all.
Cognitive capacity refers to the limited amount of mental resources, such as attention and working memory, that a person has available to think and solve problems at any given moment.
Working memory refers to the system that temporarily holds and manipulates information while a person carries out mental tasks.

This study is based on the idea of limited attentional resources (Kahneman, 1973), which proposes that people have a fixed pool of attention that must be shared between everything they are thinking about.
If part of this pool is used to resist the urge to check one's phone, less attention will be left for the task at hand, even if the person is not aware of it.
The present study asked whether the location of a person's own smartphone affects their available cognitive capacity.
It was hypothesised that the closer participants' phones were to them, the worse they would perform on tests of cognitive capacity.
The study was an experiment in which participants were randomly assigned to one of three phone-location conditions.
Participants were 520 undergraduate students at a large university in the United States who owned a smartphone.
Participants were asked to place their phone either face down on the desk, in their pocket or bag, or in another room, and all phones were set to silent with vibration turned off.

Working memory capacity was measured with the operation span task, in which participants solved simple maths problems while remembering a series of letters, with higher scores showing greater capacity.
Fluid intelligence was measured with a set of Raven's Progressive Matrices, in which participants choose the missing piece that completes a visual pattern.
Participants also answered questions about how much they felt they depended on their smartphones in daily life.

Participants whose phones were in another room had the highest working memory scores, followed by those whose phones were in their pocket or bag, and those whose phones were on the desk had the lowest scores, p < .05.
A similar pattern was found for fluid intelligence, although the differences between the groups were smaller.
The effect of phone location was strongest for participants who reported depending most on their smartphones.
Most participants said that they had not been thinking about their phones during the tasks.
These findings suggest that the mere presence of one's own smartphone reduces the mental capacity available for other tasks, even when the phone is silent and not being used.
Interestingly, most participants said they had not been thinking about their phones, which suggests that the effect may occur without people being aware of it.
This means that people may not realise how much their phones are affecting their concentration, and may therefore not take steps to reduce the problem.
The results support the idea of limited attentional resources, suggesting that ignoring a nearby phone may use up attention without people noticing.
In practice, students could leave their phones in another room when studying or sitting examinations, rather than simply switching them to silent.
One limitation is that the study was conducted with American university students, so the results may differ for older adults or people in other cultures.
Future research could test how long the effect lasts and whether it also affects learning in real classrooms.
Out of sight may indeed mean out of mind, at least when it comes to smartphones.

title: Counting Blessings or Burdens: An Experimental Study of Gratitude, Well-Being and Physical Health in Daily Life
based_on: Emmons, R. A., & McCullough, M. E. (2003). Counting blessings versus burdens: An experimental investigation of gratitude and subjective well-being in daily life. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 84(2), 377–389. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.84.2.377

s: Gratitude has long been praised by philosophers and religious traditions, yet relatively few studies have examined whether deliberately practising gratitude changes how people feel.
In this experiment, undergraduate students were randomly assigned to one of three conditions in which they wrote weekly about things they were grateful for, daily hassles, or neutral life events.
Participants completed the weekly records for ten weeks and reported their well-being, physical symptoms and health behaviours each week.
Compared with the hassles and neutral-events conditions, participants in the gratitude condition rated their lives more favourably as a whole and felt more optimistic about the upcoming week.
They also reported fewer physical complaints and spent more time exercising.
However, gratitude did not reliably increase day-to-day positive mood.
These findings suggest that a brief and inexpensive gratitude exercise may produce meaningful benefits for well-being and health.
Over the past two decades, psychologists have become increasingly interested in positive emotions and the conditions under which people flourish.
Among the positive emotions, gratitude has received growing attention because it appears to be closely tied to how people relate to others and to their own lives.
Gratitude has been described as a 'moral emotion' because it often follows help from others and may motivate people to return kindness in the future.
Many cultures also treat gratitude as a virtue, encouraging children from an early age to say 'thank you' and to appreciate what they have.
Despite this long history, psychology has traditionally paid far more attention to negative emotions, such as anxiety and depression, than to positive ones.

In this study, gratitude is defined as a sense of thankfulness and appreciation that arises when a person recognises that they have received something of value, whether from another person or from life in general.
Subjective well-being refers to a person's own evaluation of their life, including their overall life satisfaction and the balance of positive and negative feelings they experience.
Correlational studies have found that people who describe themselves as grateful tend to report higher life satisfaction, more optimism and less depression than people who are less grateful.
For example, adults who scored highly on a measure of grateful disposition reported more positive emotions and were rated by their friends as more helpful and supportive.
Grateful people have also been found to report less envy and to be less focused on material possessions than less grateful people.
Some researchers have suggested that these patterns may reflect personality, since people who are high in agreeableness also tend to be more grateful.
Others have argued that gratitude acts as a buffer against stress, because people who notice the good things in their lives may cope better when things go wrong.

Because these studies measured gratitude and well-being at the same time, however, they cannot show whether gratitude leads to greater well-being or whether happier people simply find it easier to feel grateful.
To date, very few studies have experimentally manipulated gratitude to test whether it produces changes in well-being over time.
One theoretical explanation for why gratitude may be beneficial comes from the broaden-and-build theory of positive emotions (Fredrickson, 2001).

According to this theory, positive emotions broaden people's momentary thinking and encourage them to build lasting personal resources, such as social bonds and coping skills, which in turn support well-being and health.
If gratitude works in this way, regularly directing attention to the good things in life should, over time, improve how people evaluate their lives and may even encourage healthier behaviour.
It is also possible that focusing on hassles has the opposite effect, because dwelling on problems may narrow attention to what is going wrong.
An alternative account is that any form of regular reflection, whether positive or negative, might increase well-being simply by helping people organise their thoughts about their week.
Including a neutral comparison condition therefore allows the effect of gratitude to be separated from the effect of reflection in general.

The present study therefore asked whether regularly counting one's blessings, compared with counting one's burdens or simply describing life events, would lead to greater well-being and better physical health.

It was hypothesised that participants in the gratitude condition would report greater overall life satisfaction and more optimism about the coming week than participants in the hassles and events conditions.

It was further hypothesised that participants in the gratitude condition would report fewer physical symptoms and more healthy behaviours, such as exercise, than participants in the other two conditions.
No specific prediction was made about day-to-day mood, which was examined as an exploratory outcome.
The study used an experimental design in which participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions for a period of ten weeks.

Participants were 192 undergraduate students (128 women, 64 men; mean age = 19.6 years) enrolled in an introductory psychology course at a large public university in the United States, who took part in exchange for course credit.

Each week, participants in the gratitude condition listed up to five things in their lives that they were grateful or thankful for, participants in the hassles condition listed up to five daily hassles that had annoyed or irritated them, and participants in the events condition listed up to five events that had affected them in the past week.

Example responses in the gratitude condition included "waking up this morning" and "the generosity of friends", whereas examples in the hassles condition included "finding parking" and "messy kitchen no one will clean".
The events condition served as a comparison group because it asked participants to reflect on their week without directing them towards either positive or negative content.
After writing their lists, all participants completed the same set of weekly questionnaires.
Overall life appraisal was measured with a single item asking participants to rate their life as a whole during the past week on a 7-point scale ranging from 1 (terrible) to 7 (delighted).
Optimism was measured by asking participants how they expected to feel about the upcoming week, also on a 7-point scale.

Physical symptoms were measured with a checklist of common complaints, such as headaches, stomach aches, muscle pain and coughing, on which participants indicated how often they had experienced each symptom in the past week.
Participants also reported the number of hours they had spent exercising during the week.
Positive and negative mood were measured with a list of 30 adjectives, such as "excited", "grateful", "irritable" and "sad", which participants rated on a 6-point scale.
To check that the manipulation worked, participants also rated how grateful they had felt during the week.
Participants in the gratitude condition reported feeling more grateful than participants in the other two conditions, indicating that the manipulation was successful.

Across the ten weeks, participants in the gratitude condition rated their lives as a whole more favourably (M = 5.48) than participants in the hassles (M = 4.98) and events (M = 5.05) conditions, F(2, 189) = 5.84, p = .003.

Participants in the gratitude condition were also more optimistic about the coming week (M = 5.25) than those in the hassles condition (M = 4.86), p = .01, although they did not differ significantly from the events condition, p = .09.

Participants in the gratitude condition reported fewer physical symptoms than those in the other conditions, F(2, 189) = 3.97, p = .02, and spent nearly 1.5 more hours per week exercising than participants in the hassles condition, p = .03.
For daily mood, the three conditions did not differ significantly in positive affect, F(2, 189) = 1.36, p = .26, or negative affect, F(2, 189) = 0.82, p = .44.
The effects on life appraisal and physical symptoms were small to moderate in size.
Women and men did not differ in their responses to the gratitude exercise, and the pattern of results was similar across the ten weeks of the study.
The hassles and events conditions did not differ significantly from each other on any outcome.
This study found that a simple weekly gratitude exercise led to more favourable evaluations of life and fewer physical complaints over a ten-week period.
These results extend earlier correlational research by showing that gratitude is not merely a feature of happy people but can be deliberately practised, with measurable benefits.
Theoretically, the findings support the broaden-and-build theory by suggesting that a positive emotion such as gratitude may build resources that benefit both psychological and physical well-being.
The absence of an effect on daily mood suggests that gratitude may influence how people evaluate their lives more than how they feel from moment to moment.
The finding that the events condition did not differ from the hassles condition also suggests that the benefits came from gratitude specifically, rather than from reflection in general.
One possible reason for the health effects is that people who feel more positive about their lives may have more energy and motivation to look after their bodies, for instance by exercising.
These findings are consistent with research showing that positive emotions are associated with better immune functioning and fewer illnesses.
In practice, counsellors and educators could introduce brief gratitude journals as a low-cost activity to support students' well-being, particularly during stressful periods such as examinations.

Several limitations should be noted, however, as the sample consisted only of undergraduate psychology students from one American university, which limits how far the findings can be generalised to other age groups and cultures.
In addition, all outcomes were self-reported, so participants' answers may have been influenced by their expectations about the study.
Future research could use objective measures of health, such as fitness trackers or medical records, and could test whether the benefits of gratitude last after people stop keeping a journal.
Overall, the findings suggest that counting one's blessings is a simple practice that may make a meaningful difference to how people view their lives.

title: Less Scrolling, Less Loneliness? An Experiment on Limiting Social Media Use Among University Students
based_on: Hunt, M. G., Marx, R., Lipson, C., & Young, J. (2018). No more FOMO: Limiting social media decreases loneliness and depression. Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology, 37(10), 751–768. https://doi.org/10.1521/jscp.2018.37.10.751

s: Many studies have linked heavy social media use with poorer mental health, but most have relied on correlational designs and self-estimated screen time.
This study tested experimentally whether limiting social media use would improve the well-being of university students.
After a baseline week, 143 undergraduates were randomly assigned either to limit Facebook, Instagram and Snapchat to 10 minutes per platform per day or to use social media as usual for three weeks.
Social media use was measured objectively using screenshots of each participant's phone battery usage screen.

Students who limited their use showed significantly larger decreases in loneliness and depression than students in the usual-use group, and the reduction in depression was strongest among students who started the study with higher levels of depression.
Both groups showed similar reductions in anxiety and fear of missing out, which may reflect the benefits of simply monitoring one's own use.
The findings suggest that reducing, rather than eliminating, social media use may benefit students' mental health.
Social media platforms such as Facebook, Instagram and Snapchat have become a central part of daily life for most university students, many of whom check their accounts dozens of times a day.
These platforms allow students to stay in touch with friends and family, share experiences and join communities with similar interests.
At the same time, concerns have grown that heavy use may harm young people's mental health, particularly during the transition to university, when many students feel isolated.
Loneliness refers to the distressing feeling that one's social relationships are fewer or less satisfying than one would like.
Depression, in this study, refers to a persistent low mood accompanied by symptoms such as loss of interest, poor sleep, low energy and feelings of worthlessness.
Fear of missing out (FOMO) refers to the worry that others are having rewarding experiences from which one is absent, together with a desire to stay continually connected with what others are doing.
Large survey studies have found that young adults who spend more time on social media tend to report more loneliness and depressive symptoms (Primack et al., 2017).
Similar associations have been reported between social media use and anxiety, poor sleep and lower self-esteem.

However, because these studies were correlational, they cannot tell us whether social media use leads to poorer mental health or whether people who are already lonely and depressed simply spend more time online.
In addition, most earlier studies relied on participants' own estimates of their screen time, which research has shown to be inaccurate and often biased.
A small number of studies have asked participants to quit Facebook completely for a week, but quitting entirely is unrealistic for most students and the effects of a single week may not last.

One explanation for the link between social media and poorer well-being comes from social comparison theory (Festinger, 1954), which proposes that people evaluate their own lives and abilities by comparing themselves with others.
On social media, users mostly see carefully selected, positive images of others' lives, which may lead to upward comparisons in which people feel that their own lives are less exciting or successful.
Displacement is a second possible mechanism, as time spent scrolling may replace face-to-face interaction, sleep or other activities that protect mental health.
The present study aimed to test experimentally whether limiting social media use, measured objectively, would improve students' well-being over three weeks.
It was hypothesised that students who limited their social media use would show a greater decrease in loneliness than students who continued to use social media as usual.
It was also hypothesised that students who limited their use would show a greater decrease in depression than students in the usual-use group.
Finally, because limiting use might reduce social comparison, it was predicted that the limited-use group would show greater reductions in anxiety and FOMO.
The study used a randomised experimental design with two conditions and measurements taken before and after the three-week intervention.

Participants were 143 undergraduate students (108 women, 35 men) at a private university in the north-eastern United States, who owned an iPhone and had active Facebook, Instagram and Snapchat accounts.
Participants were recruited through the psychology department's research pool and received course credit for taking part.
During the first week, all participants used social media as normal so that baseline levels of use and well-being could be recorded.
Social media use was measured objectively: each evening, participants sent the researchers screenshots of their iPhone battery usage screen, which shows the number of minutes spent in each app.

Participants were then randomly assigned to either a limited-use condition, in which they were asked to spend no more than 10 minutes per platform per day (about 30 minutes in total), or a usual-use condition, in which they continued to use social media as they normally would.
Participants in the limited-use condition were encouraged to use their phone's built-in settings to remind them when they reached their daily limit.

Loneliness was measured with the revised UCLA Loneliness Scale, a 20-item questionnaire in which participants rate statements such as "I lack companionship" on a 4-point scale, with higher scores indicating greater loneliness.
Depression was measured with the Beck Depression Inventory, a widely used 21-item measure of depressive symptoms.
Anxiety was measured with the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory, and FOMO was measured with the 10-item Fear of Missing Out Scale.
All well-being measures were completed at baseline and again at the end of the three-week period.
Thirteen participants were excluded because they did not submit their usage screenshots on most days, leaving a final sample of 130 for the analyses.

Participants in the limited-use condition reduced their total social media use substantially, from an average of about 78 minutes per day at baseline to about 30 minutes per day, whereas use in the usual-use condition remained similar.
Loneliness decreased significantly more in the limited-use condition than in the usual-use condition, F(1, 128) = 6.42, p = .01.
Depression also decreased significantly more in the limited-use condition, F(1, 128) = 5.11, p = .03.
Further analysis showed that this reduction in depression was largest among participants who had reported higher levels of depression at baseline.
Both conditions showed significant decreases in anxiety and FOMO from baseline to the end of the study, but the two conditions did not differ from each other on these outcomes, both ps > .30.
There were no significant differences between conditions in social support, self-esteem or self-acceptance.
The results indicate that limiting social media use to around 30 minutes per day led to meaningful reductions in loneliness and depression over three weeks.

Because participants were randomly assigned and use was measured objectively, these findings provide stronger evidence than earlier correlational studies that social media use may contribute to poorer well-being.

Theoretically, the findings are consistent with social comparison theory, as reducing exposure to idealised images of others' lives may reduce unfavourable comparisons and the negative feelings they produce.
The finding that anxiety and FOMO decreased in both conditions suggests that simply monitoring one's own social media use each day may increase self-awareness and bring some benefits on its own.
The stronger effect for students who began the study with higher depression suggests that the intervention may be most helpful for those who are already struggling.

In practice, university counselling services could encourage students to set daily time limits on social media rather than asking them to give it up completely, which many students would find unrealistic.
One limitation is that the study only included iPhone users from a single private university, and the sample was mostly female, so the findings may not apply to other groups of students.
Another limitation is that the study lasted only three weeks, so it is unclear whether the benefits would continue if students kept limiting their use.

Future research should follow participants for longer periods and should examine which specific features of social media, such as viewing others' photos or receiving comments, are most strongly linked to loneliness and depression.
Taken together, the findings suggest that using social media less, rather than not at all, may be a practical way for students to look after their mental health.

title: Short-Term Relief, Long-Term Cost: A Semester-Long Study of Procrastination, Stress, Health and Academic Performance
based_on: Tice, D. M., & Baumeister, R. F. (1997). Longitudinal study of procrastination, performance, stress, and health: The costs and benefits of dawdling. Psychological Science, 8(6), 454–458. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.1997.tb00460.x

s: Procrastination is common among university students, yet its consequences for well-being remain debated.
Some students claim that they work best under pressure and that putting off work reduces stress, whereas others believe that procrastination is harmful.
This study followed undergraduate students across a full semester to examine how procrastination was related to stress, physical illness and academic performance at different points in time.
Early in the semester, students who scored higher on procrastination reported less stress and fewer symptoms of illness than students who scored lower.
By the end of the semester, however, this pattern had reversed: procrastinators reported more stress and more symptoms, and they received lower grades on their assignments and examinations.
Across the whole semester, procrastination was associated with greater overall stress and illness.
These results suggest that procrastination is a self-defeating behaviour pattern that offers short-term relief but carries long-term costs.
Procrastination refers to the voluntary delay of an intended course of action despite expecting to be worse off as a result of the delay.

It is one of the most common problems reported by university students, with surveys suggesting that a large majority of undergraduates procrastinate at least some of the time and many consider it a serious problem.
Despite how common it is, students disagree about whether procrastination is actually harmful.
Some students argue that leaving work until the last minute helps them focus, because the pressure of a deadline increases their motivation and efficiency.
Others report that procrastination makes them anxious and leads to rushed, lower-quality work.
Previous research has produced mixed findings on this question.
Some studies have found that procrastinators obtain lower grades, while others have found little relationship between procrastination and performance once ability is taken into account.
Importantly, most earlier studies measured procrastination and its outcomes only once, so they could not show whether the costs and benefits of procrastination change over time.
A single measurement taken early in a semester might show that procrastinators are relaxed, whereas a measurement taken just before deadlines might show the opposite.

The present research draws on the idea of self-defeating behaviour (Baumeister & Scher, 1988), which describes patterns in which people pursue an immediate benefit at the expense of a larger delayed cost.

According to this view, people engage in self-defeating behaviours because the benefit, such as relief from an unpleasant task, is felt immediately, whereas the cost, such as poorer performance and stress, comes later and is easier to ignore.

If procrastination is a self-defeating behaviour, procrastinators should feel better than others early in the semester, when deadlines are far away, but worse than others later, when the delayed work must finally be completed.
Stress, in this study, refers to the feeling that the demands placed on a person exceed their ability to cope.
The present study therefore asked how procrastination is related to stress, illness and academic performance at the beginning and end of a semester.
It was hypothesised that students higher in procrastination would report less stress and fewer illness symptoms than other students early in the semester.
It was further hypothesised that, by the end of the semester, students higher in procrastination would report more stress and illness symptoms than other students.
Finally, it was predicted that procrastination would be associated with poorer academic performance.
This was a longitudinal correlational study in which the same students were measured at several points across one semester, without any manipulation by the researchers.
Participants were 44 undergraduate students enrolled in a health psychology course at a university in the United States, who took part as part of their course requirements.

Procrastination was measured in the first week of the semester using the General Procrastination Scale, a 20-item questionnaire in which participants rated statements such as "I generally delay before starting on work I have to do" on a 5-point scale.

Stress and physical illness were measured with a symptom checklist asking how often participants had experienced symptoms such as headaches, colds, stomach problems and difficulty sleeping, along with a rating of how stressed they felt.
These measures were completed in the fourth week of the semester and again in the final week, shortly before examinations.
Participants also reported the number of visits they had made to health-care professionals during the semester.
Academic performance was recorded from the course instructor's records and included marks for a term paper and for two examinations.
The deadline for the term paper was announced at the start of the semester, and the date on which each paper was submitted was also recorded as an objective indicator of procrastination.
To check that any differences were not simply due to academic ability, participants' prior grade point averages were also obtained.
Scores on the procrastination scale were positively correlated with how late students handed in their term papers, r = .39, p = .01, supporting the validity of the scale.

Early in the semester, procrastination was negatively correlated with stress, r = −.33, p = .03, and with symptoms of illness, r = −.30, p = .05, meaning that procrastinators felt somewhat better at this point.
By the end of the semester, procrastination was positively correlated with stress, r = .29, p = .06, and with symptoms of illness, r = .31, p = .04.
Procrastinators also reported more visits to health-care professionals across the semester.
Procrastination was negatively correlated with term paper grades, r = −.42, p = .01, and with examination grades, r = −.37, p = .02.
These relationships with grades remained significant after controlling for students' prior grade point averages.
The findings show that the effects of procrastination depend on when they are measured.
Early in the semester, procrastinators reported less stress and fewer symptoms, which may explain why many students believe that putting off work is harmless.
By the end of the semester, however, procrastinators were more stressed and more often ill, and they performed worse on both their term papers and their examinations.
Theoretically, this pattern supports the view of procrastination as a self-defeating behaviour, in which short-term relief is gained at the cost of long-term well-being and performance.
The results also challenge the popular belief that procrastinators work better under pressure, since their work was graded lower even after their prior ability was taken into account.

In practical terms, universities could teach time-management strategies early in the semester and set intermediate deadlines for large assignments, so that students do not leave all of their work until the end.
A limitation of the study is its small sample of 44 students from a single course, which reduces statistical power and makes it difficult to generalise the findings.
In addition, because the study was correlational, it cannot show that procrastination causes stress and illness; other factors, such as poor self-regulation, may influence both.
Future research could use larger and more diverse samples and could test experimentally whether interventions that reduce procrastination also reduce stress at the end of the semester.
In summary, putting off work may feel good at first, but the costs appear to catch up with students when it matters most.

title: Sleep Across the Semester: Objectively Measured Sleep Duration, Quality and Consistency and Exam Performance in University Students
based_on: Okano, K., Kaczmarzyk, J. R., Dave, N., Gabrieli, J. D. E., & Grossman, J. C. (2019). Sleep quality, duration, and consistency are associated with better academic performance in college students. npj Science of Learning, 4, Article 16. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0055-z

s: Although it is widely believed that sleep supports learning, most studies of students' sleep and grades have relied on self-reported sleep, which is often inaccurate.
This study used wearable activity trackers to measure the sleep of students in an introductory chemistry course throughout a semester.
Better sleep quality, longer sleep duration and more consistent sleep across the semester were each associated with higher scores on the course's tests.
In contrast, the amount of sleep obtained on the single night before a test was not related to test performance.
Together, sleep measures accounted for nearly a quarter of the differences between students' overall grades.
These findings suggest that consistent, good-quality sleep over weeks, rather than sleep on the night before an exam, is associated with academic success.
Many university students sleep less than the seven to nine hours recommended for young adults, especially during busy periods of the semester.
Late-night studying, social activities and irregular class schedules can all lead to short and inconsistent sleep.
At the same time, laboratory research has shown that sleep plays an important role in memory, as information learned during the day appears to be strengthened during sleep.
For example, people who sleep after learning a list of word pairs typically recall more of the pairs the next day than people who stay awake for the same length of time.
Sleep deprivation has also been shown to impair attention, working memory and mood, all of which may affect how well students learn and perform in examinations.
Outside the laboratory, however, students' sleep is influenced by many factors at once, and it is less clear how strongly everyday sleep habits are related to real academic outcomes.
In this study, sleep quality refers to how restful and uninterrupted a person's sleep is, rather than simply how long it lasts.
Sleep consistency refers to how similar a person's sleep duration and timing are from one night to the next.
Several survey studies have found that students who report sleeping more tend to obtain higher grades.
Other studies have found that students who go to bed and wake up at irregular times report poorer concentration in class.
Some researchers have also suggested that students with higher motivation may simply organise their time better, leading to both better sleep and better grades.
However, these studies mostly relied on students' own reports of how much they slept, which are known to be inaccurate and may be biased by how well students think they are doing.
Furthermore, most studies examined sleep at only one point in time, so it remains unclear whether long-term sleep habits or sleep on the night before an exam matter more for performance.
Many students believe that sleeping well the night before an exam is what matters most, while others sacrifice sleep before exams in order to study for longer.

The present study is guided by the memory consolidation account of sleep, which proposes that newly learned information is gradually stabilised and integrated into long-term memory during sleep (Diekelmann & Born, 2010).
If sleep supports learning in this way, then good sleep throughout the period in which material is being learned, rather than only before the test, should be associated with better performance.

The present study therefore asked whether objectively measured sleep duration, quality and consistency across a semester are related to students' academic performance, and whether sleep on the night before a test is related to performance on that test.
It was hypothesised that students with longer, better-quality and more consistent sleep across the semester would obtain higher test scores.
It was also hypothesised that longer sleep on the night before a test would be associated with higher scores on that particular test.
This was a correlational study in which the researchers observed students' naturally occurring sleep without asking them to change it.
Participants were 88 undergraduate students (47 women, 41 men) enrolled in an introductory chemistry course at a university in the United States.
All students in the course were invited to take part, and those who agreed received a wearable activity tracker that they were asked to wear day and night for the whole semester.
Sleep duration was measured objectively by the tracker, which recorded the number of minutes each participant slept each night.
Sleep quality was calculated from the tracker's data as the proportion of time in bed that the participant was actually asleep, with fewer awakenings indicating better quality.
Sleep consistency was calculated as how much a participant's nightly sleep duration varied from night to night, with less variation indicating greater consistency.
Academic performance was measured using students' scores on nine short quizzes, three midterm examinations and a final examination.
Because the tracker did not ask students how they felt, the researchers also collected brief information about students' year of study and whether they lived on campus.
On average, participants slept about 6 hours and 30 minutes per night, which is below the recommended amount for young adults.
Longer sleep duration across the semester was positively correlated with overall test scores, r = .38, p < .001.
Better sleep quality was also positively correlated with overall scores, r = .40, p < .001, as was greater sleep consistency, r = .36, p = .001.
Together, sleep duration, quality and consistency accounted for nearly 25% of the variation in students' overall grades.
In contrast, the amount of sleep obtained on the night before each test was not significantly related to scores on that test, r = .07, p = .48.
Women tended to have better sleep quality than men, but the relationships between sleep and grades were similar for both groups.
This study found that students who slept longer, better and more consistently over the semester tended to perform better on their tests.
The size of these relationships was notable, given that grades are also influenced by many other factors, such as prior knowledge, motivation and study habits.
The finding that students slept on average only six and a half hours per night also suggests that many students may be regularly sleep-deprived during the semester.
However, sleep on the night immediately before a test was not related to performance on that test.

These findings are consistent with the memory consolidation account, as they suggest that sleep supports learning over the weeks in which material is studied, rather than only on the night before it is tested.

In practice, universities could include education about regular sleep habits in orientation programmes and could avoid scheduling early-morning classes or late-night deadlines that disrupt students' sleep.
Students may also benefit from treating good sleep as part of their study routine throughout the semester, rather than trying to catch up on sleep just before examinations.
Because the study was correlational, it cannot show that better sleep causes better grades; for example, students who are more organised may both sleep more regularly and study more effectively.
The sample was also limited to students in one chemistry course at a single university, so the results may not apply to students in other subjects or countries.
Future research could test whether interventions that improve students' sleep consistency lead to improvements in their grades, which would provide stronger evidence about cause and effect.
Overall, these findings suggest that good sleep habits across the semester are closely linked to academic success.

title: Scrolling and Feeling: Facebook Use Predicts Declines in Momentary Affect and Life Satisfaction in Young Adults
short: Facebook use and well-being over two weeks
based_on: Kross, E., Verduyn, P., Demiralp, E., Park, J., Lee, D. S., Lin, N., Shablack, H., Jonides, J., & Ybarra, O. (2013). Facebook use predicts declines in subjective well-being in young adults. PLOS ONE, 8(8), Article e69841. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0069841

s: Over a billion people use Facebook, which offers an unprecedented opportunity to satisfy the basic human need for social connection.
Rather than enhancing well-being, however, the present findings suggest that Facebook use may undermine it.

Young adults were sent text messages five times per day for two weeks, asking how they felt, how worried and lonely they were, and how much they had used Facebook and interacted directly with other people since the previous message.

Multilevel analyses indicated that the more people used Facebook at one time point, the worse they felt at the next time point, and the more they used Facebook over the two weeks, the more their life satisfaction declined.
Direct interactions with other people did not predict declines in well-being.
There was no evidence that feeling bad led people to use Facebook more, and the effects were not explained by loneliness, gender, self-esteem or depression.
These results suggest that, on the surface, Facebook provides an invaluable resource for fulfilling the need for connection, but it may in fact have the opposite effect on young adults' well-being.
Facebook allows people to stay in contact with friends and family, share news and photographs and receive social support, all at any time of the day.
Because humans have a fundamental need to belong, a tool that makes social contact so easy might be expected to increase well-being.
Research on social relationships consistently shows that people with strong social ties are happier, healthier and live longer than people who are socially isolated.
Online communication might therefore be expected to bring the same benefits as face-to-face contact, particularly for people who find it difficult to meet others in person.
On the other hand, online interaction differs from face-to-face interaction in important ways, for example because it lacks facial expressions, tone of voice and physical touch.
Subjective well-being refers to how people evaluate their lives, and it is usually separated into two components.
The first component, affective well-being, refers to how people feel from moment to moment, including the balance of their positive and negative emotions.
The second component, cognitive well-being, refers to people's overall judgement of how satisfied they are with their lives.
Previous research on Facebook and well-being has produced mixed results.
Some studies have found that Facebook use is associated with greater social capital and higher self-esteem, particularly among people who feel insecure in face-to-face settings.
Other studies have found that heavier Facebook users report more loneliness, more envy and lower life satisfaction.
For instance, one survey of university students found that those who spent more time on Facebook were more likely to agree that other people had better lives than they did.
Another study found that passively browsing other people's profiles was associated with greater envy, whereas actively posting and messaging were not.
These mixed findings suggest that the relationship between Facebook use and well-being may depend on how, when and by whom Facebook is used.
A key problem is that almost all of this research has been cross-sectional, measuring Facebook use and well-being at a single point in time.
Cross-sectional designs cannot show how Facebook use and well-being relate to each other over time, or whether Facebook use comes before changes in well-being or follows them.
In addition, most studies have asked people to estimate their Facebook use over long periods, which requires them to remember behaviour that is frequent, brief and easy to forget.
Experience sampling, in which people are repeatedly asked about their current experiences in daily life, offers a way to address both of these problems.

One theoretical reason to expect Facebook use to harm well-being comes from social comparison theory (Festinger, 1954), which proposes that people evaluate themselves by comparing their own lives and abilities with those of others.
Because users tend to post flattering information, frequent exposure to others' highlights may lead to upward comparisons and feelings of envy and inadequacy.
At the same time, it is possible that the relationship works in the opposite direction, so that people who already feel bad turn to Facebook to cheer themselves up.

It is also possible that a third variable, such as loneliness or low self-esteem, leads people both to use Facebook more and to feel worse, which would make the two appear related even if one does not influence the other.
A design that measures both variables repeatedly over time allows researchers to test whether Facebook use comes before changes in well-being, while also taking such third variables into account.
The present study therefore examined how Facebook use influences the two components of subjective well-being over time in young adults.
It was hypothesised that greater Facebook use at one time point would predict worse affect at the next time point.
It was further hypothesised that greater Facebook use across the two-week period would predict declines in life satisfaction from the start to the end of the study.
In contrast, it was predicted that direct (face-to-face or telephone) interaction with other people would not predict declines in well-being.
The study used an experience-sampling design, in which participants' Facebook use and well-being were measured repeatedly in daily life over two weeks without any manipulation by the researchers.
Participants were 82 young adults (53 women, 29 men; mean age = 19.5 years) from a university town in the Midwestern United States, all of whom had a Facebook account and a smartphone.
They were recruited through flyers and were paid for their participation.
At the start of the study, participants completed questionnaires measuring life satisfaction, depression, self-esteem, loneliness and the number of their Facebook friends.
Over the following 14 days, participants received five text messages per day at random times between 10 a.m. and midnight.

Each text message linked to a short online survey in which participants rated how they felt "right now" on a slider scale from "very positive" to "very negative", which served as the measure of affect.
Each survey also asked participants how much they had used Facebook since the last survey, on a scale from 1 (not at all) to 5 (a lot).
Direct social interaction was measured by asking how much participants had interacted with other people "directly" (face-to-face or on the phone) since the last survey, on the same 5-point scale.
Participants also rated how worried and how lonely they felt at each survey.

At the end of the 14 days, participants again completed the Satisfaction with Life Scale, a 5-item questionnaire in which they rate statements such as "I am satisfied with my life" on a 7-point scale.
Participants responded to an average of 83% of the text messages, indicating good compliance.
Because each participant provided many responses, the data were analysed using multilevel models, which take into account that responses from the same person are related to each other.
The more participants used Facebook between two text messages, the worse they felt at the second text message, B = −0.08, SE = 0.03, p = .003.
However, how participants felt at one text message did not predict how much they used Facebook before the next text message, B = 0.002, p = .90.
In contrast, the more participants interacted directly with other people, the better they felt over time, B = 0.08, p = .03.
The more participants used Facebook over the two weeks, the more their life satisfaction declined from the start to the end of the study, B = −0.41, p = .006.
Direct social interaction was not significantly related to changes in life satisfaction, B = 0.10, p = .57.
Loneliness was associated with greater Facebook use, B = 0.15, p < .001, but loneliness did not account for the relationship between Facebook use and declines in affect.
The relationship between Facebook use and affect did not differ according to participants' gender, self-esteem, depression or the size of their Facebook network.
These findings suggest that Facebook use predicts declines in both how people feel from moment to moment and how satisfied they are with their lives.
Importantly, there was no evidence that people used Facebook more when they felt bad, which makes it less likely that the results simply reflect unhappy people turning to Facebook.

The finding that direct interaction did not have the same negative effect suggests that it is not social contact in general that undermines well-being, but something specific about interacting through Facebook.

Several features of Facebook could explain this difference, including the tendency to present an idealised version of oneself, the large number of weak ties in most users' networks, and the ease of passively observing others without interacting.

The finding that loneliness predicted greater Facebook use, but did not explain its relationship with affect, suggests that lonely people may turn to Facebook for connection without receiving the benefits they are seeking.

Theoretically, these findings extend social comparison theory to everyday online behaviour, suggesting that frequent exposure to others' selectively positive posts may gradually reduce people's evaluations of their own lives.
The results also challenge the assumption that tools which make social contact easier necessarily satisfy the human need for connection.

Practically, students and counsellors should be aware that frequent Facebook use may lower mood, and young people could be encouraged to balance online contact with direct interaction with friends and family.
One limitation is that, although the design tracked how variables changed over time, it was not experimental, so it cannot establish that Facebook use causes declines in well-being.
Facebook use was also self-reported, and participants may not have estimated their use accurately even over short periods.
In addition, the sample was relatively small and consisted mainly of university students in one region of the United States.

Future research should experimentally manipulate Facebook use, for example by asking some participants to stop using it for a period, and should examine which specific activities on Facebook, such as passively scrolling versus posting, are responsible for these effects.
Taken together, the findings suggest that, rather than enhancing well-being, interacting with Facebook may predict the opposite outcome for young adults.

title: Testing Versus Restudying: The Effect of Retrieval Practice on Short- and Long-Term Recall of Prose Passages
based_on: Roediger, H. L., III, & Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science, 17(3), 249–255. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2006.01693.x

s: Tests are usually seen as tools for measuring what students have learned, rather than as a way to improve learning.
In this experiment, students read short prose passages and then either restudied each passage or took a free-recall test on it, without receiving feedback.
Final recall was tested after 5 minutes, 2 days or 1 week.
After 5 minutes, restudying produced slightly better recall than testing, but after 2 days and 1 week, testing produced substantially better recall than restudying.
Students who restudied also predicted that they would remember more than students who were tested, even though the opposite was true in the long term.
These findings show that taking a test is a powerful learning event and that students may underestimate its benefits.
Most students prepare for examinations by rereading their notes and textbooks, often several times.
Surveys of study habits show that rereading is among the most popular study strategies, while practising recall without looking at one's notes is used much less often.
In education, tests are usually treated as neutral assessments that measure learning without changing it.
Students and teachers often view tests as stressful events that interrupt learning, and many students try to avoid practice tests until they feel fully prepared.
Teachers, in turn, may limit the number of quizzes they give because of the time needed to prepare and mark them.
If testing itself improves learning, however, these practices may be preventing students from using one of the most effective learning strategies available.

However, laboratory research has identified the testing effect, which refers to the finding that retrieving information from memory improves later retention of that information more than spending the same time restudying it.
Retrieval practice, in turn, refers to any learning activity in which a learner deliberately recalls information from memory, such as answering questions or writing down everything they can remember.
Early demonstrations of the testing effect date back nearly a century, when schoolchildren who recited material from memory remembered it better than those who only reread it.
Since then, many laboratory studies have shown that people who are tested on word lists or word pairs remember them better on a later test than people who simply study the same items again.
Some researchers have argued that this benefit occurs only because testing gives learners extra exposure to the material, in the same way as restudying would.
Others have argued that the benefit occurs only when learners receive feedback, which tells them the correct answers they failed to retrieve.
Neither explanation can be tested unless the time spent on testing and restudying is equal and no feedback is given.

Despite this long history, most studies of the testing effect have used simple materials, such as lists of unrelated words, rather than the kind of connected prose that students read in their courses.
In addition, many studies measured memory only shortly after learning, so it is not clear whether the benefits of testing last over the delays that typically separate studying from examinations.
Another unanswered question is whether students are aware of the benefits of testing, which may help to explain why they rarely use it.

One explanation for the testing effect is the retrieval effort account (Bjork, 1994), which proposes that the act of effortfully retrieving information strengthens memory and creates more routes for accessing it later.

According to this account, restudying feels easier because the information is in front of the learner, but this ease does not produce the same lasting strengthening of memory as retrieving the information unaided.

This account also suggests that the benefit of testing may not appear immediately, because restudying gives learners extra exposure to the material just before the test, which may help them in the short term.

The present study asked whether taking a test on a prose passage, compared with restudying it, leads to better recall shortly after learning and after longer delays, and whether students can predict which strategy will help them more.
It was predicted that students who took a test would recall more of the passage than students who restudied it at all three retention intervals.
It was further predicted that the advantage of testing over restudying would increase as the delay between learning and the final test became longer.
Finally, it was expected that students who restudied would predict higher future recall than students who were tested, because rereading creates a feeling of familiarity.

The study used an experiment with a mixed design, in which learning condition (test vs restudy) was manipulated within participants and retention interval (5 minutes, 2 days or 1 week) was manipulated between participants.
Participants were 120 undergraduate students at Washington University in St. Louis, who took part for course credit or payment.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of the three retention-interval groups, with 40 students in each group.
Two prose passages from a reading-comprehension test were used, one about sea otters and one about the Sun, each about 275 words long and each divided into 30 idea units for scoring.

In the study phase, participants read each passage for 7 minutes, and then either reread the same passage for a further 7 minutes (restudy condition) or spent 7 minutes writing down as much of the passage as they could remember (test condition).
No feedback was given in the test condition, so participants in that condition were never shown the passage a second time.
Which passage was restudied and which was tested was counterbalanced across participants, so that any differences in passage difficulty could not explain the results.
After the study phase, participants solved simple maths problems for two minutes to prevent them from rehearsing the passages.
At the end of the study phase, participants rated how much of each passage they expected to remember in one week, on a scale from 1 to 7.

Final recall was measured by asking participants to write down everything they could remember from each passage, and recall was scored as the percentage of the 30 idea units that each participant correctly reproduced.
Two independent raters scored a sample of the recall protocols, and their scores agreed closely, indicating that the scoring was reliable.
After 5 minutes, participants recalled slightly more of the restudied passage (81%) than of the tested passage (75%), t(39) = 2.12, p = .04.
After 2 days, participants recalled more of the tested passage (68%) than of the restudied passage (54%), t(39) = 4.20, p < .001.
After 1 week, participants again recalled more of the tested passage (56%) than of the restudied passage (42%), t(39) = 4.59, p < .001.
A significant interaction between learning condition and retention interval, F(2, 117) = 18.9, p < .001, showed that the effect of testing depended on the delay before the final test.

Forgetting was much faster after restudying than after testing: from 5 minutes to 1 week, recall of the restudied passage dropped by 39 percentage points, whereas recall of the tested passage dropped by 19 percentage points.
Participants predicted that they would remember more of the restudied passage (M = 4.8) than of the tested passage (M = 4.0), p < .01.
These results show that taking a single recall test on a prose passage produced better long-term retention than restudying it, even though no feedback was provided.
The short-term advantage of restudying, followed by a long-term advantage of testing, shows that the benefits of a learning strategy cannot be judged from performance immediately after learning.
This pattern is important because students often judge the success of their studying by how well they feel they know the material at the end of a study session.
Because restudying produces a strong feeling of familiarity, students may conclude that it is working, even though the material will be forgotten more quickly.
The results also show that the benefits of testing did not depend on feedback, since participants in the test condition never saw the passage again after the first reading.

Theoretically, the results support the retrieval effort account, as the effortful act of retrieval appeared to slow forgetting, while the extra exposure provided by restudying produced only a brief benefit.
The finding that students expected restudying to be more effective suggests that learners may confuse the feeling that material is familiar with actually having learned it.

In practice, teachers could replace some review sessions with low-stakes quizzes, and students could test themselves, for example by using flashcards or writing summaries from memory, instead of simply rereading their notes.

One limitation is that the passages were short and the final test used the same format as the practice test, so it remains unclear whether the benefits would transfer to longer course materials or to different kinds of examination questions.
In addition, the participants were students at a selective American university, who may differ from other learners in their reading and study skills.
Future studies could examine the testing effect with real course content in classroom settings and could test whether providing feedback after practice tests increases the benefits further.
In conclusion, tests are not only a way of measuring learning but also a powerful way of producing it.
